title: Dinosaurs
strapline: Enormous names, enormous creatures — roaring, sorting and digging our way back millions of years.
intent: Build ambitious vocabulary — children who can say 'Tyrannosaurus' can say anything, and words like herbivore, carnivore, fossil and extinct come free with the play.
Compare and order by size, length and features: dinosaurs beg to be lined up, measured and argued over.
Introduce deep time gently — the idea that dinosaurs lived long, long ago, before people, and we know about them from fossils in the ground.
Sort and classify by real criteria: plant-eaters and meat-eaters, two legs and four, spikes, plates, wings.
Fuel imaginative storytelling — nests, hatching eggs, volcanoes, a Triceratops who has lost her herd.
implementation: Learn the real names and use them — children delight in polysyllables; never dumb 'Diplodocus' down to 'the long-neck one'.
Set up a dig: bury 'fossils' (cleaned bones, shells, plastic skeletons) in the sand tray with brushes and sieves, and model how a palaeontologist works slowly and records finds.
Wonder aloud rather than lecture: 'I wonder why this one's teeth are flat and that one's are sharp…' and let children build the herbivore/carnivore theory themselves.
Offer non-fiction books alongside the figures so children can match their dinosaur to the page and check its facts.
Provide natural loose parts — bark, pebbles, ferns, logs — so children build habitats rather than playing on an empty carpet.
Mark out a life-size footprint or a metre of 'Diplodocus neck' with tape so big numbers become something you can walk along.
When a child announces a dinosaur 'fact', ask how we could check — modelling that we find things out, we don't just guess.
key_questions: How do we know dinosaurs were real if nobody ever saw one?
What do you think this dinosaur ate — and what makes you say that?
Which of these dinosaurs would win a race? Which would win at hiding?
What might be inside this egg, and how should we look after it until it hatches?
Where has your dinosaur's herd gone — what's your plan to find them?

impact.text: Children use ambitious dinosaur vocabulary with relish — Triceratops, Stegosaurus, herbivore, carnivore, fossil — and carry it into other play.
Children sort the dinosaurs by real features — meat-eaters and plant-eaters, spikes or no spikes, two legs or four — and explain their groupings.
Children compare and order dinosaurs by size and length — 'Diplodocus is longer than the whole shelf' — reaching for comparative words unprompted.
Children ask genuine questions about extinction and deep time — 'why did they all die?', 'were there dinosaurs when Grandma was little?' — and expect real answers.
Children sustain shared dinosaur narratives — hatching eggs, escaping the volcano, protecting the nest — negotiating who is which dinosaur.
Children retell favourite dinosaur stories with the figures as props, adding their own twists to the ending.
Children excavate buried 'fossils' slowly and carefully, talking about what the bones might tell us and how digging changes what we can see.
Children count spikes, teeth, eggs in the nest and dinosaurs in the herd, trusting the last number as the answer.

enhancements: A fossil dig tray: plaster-of-Paris 'bones', brushes, sieves, magnifying glasses and a clipboard for recording finds.
Frozen dinosaur eggs — figures set in ice — with warm water, salt and pipettes for the rescue.
A measuring basket: string, tape measures and metre sticks to lay out real dinosaur footprint sizes on the floor.
Herbs, ferns and salad leaves as swamp planting, so herbivores have something genuine to graze.
Non-fiction dinosaur books and a 'dinosaur register' for children to tick off which species visited today.
A small-world volcano of dough over a pot, ready for a bicarbonate-and-vinegar eruption at group time.
Clay for pressing dinosaur footprints and making your own 'fossils' to bury for a friend.

playing_exploring: Children investigate the figures closely — turning them over, comparing teeth and tails — before the story even starts.
The dig tray invites open-ended exploration with no right answer: what's under here, and what is it?
active_learning: Excavating a buried fossil properly takes patience — brushing sand away slowly is its own reward.
Children persist in ordering the whole herd by size, restarting when a new dinosaur joins.
creating_thinking: Children build their own theories — flat teeth eat plants, sharp teeth eat meat — and test them against every new figure.
Story problems (the volcano is erupting, the nest is unguarded) push children to invent plans and rescue routes.
